commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:linter-driven-development
commands.description:
(go-linter-driven-development) META ORCHESTRATOR for any Go code change that should end in a commit (features, bug fixes, refactors).
WHEN: User requests Go code work (implement, fix, add, refactor), mentions "@ldd"/"ldd", or runs a /go-ldd-* command in a Go project.
Runs the five-phase workflow (PREPARE is an autonomous sub-phase, 1.5): DESIGN → PREPARE → IMPLEMENT (per-behavior TDD loop) → FULL LINT (lint-fixer agent) → REVIEW (per slice) → SHIP.

commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:pre-commit-review

(go-linter-driven-development) ADVISORY pre-commit review that orchestrates parallel single-obsession rule hunters, an over-abstraction skeptic, and a comment critic against the diff.
Spawns read-only agents (rule-hunter, overabstraction-skeptic, comment-critic); NEVER edits code.
Invoked by @linter-driven-development (Phase 4), by @refactoring (after pattern application), or manually for standalone code review.
Categorizes findings as Bugs, New Practice (when in Rome), Design Debt, Readability Debt, or Polish Opportunities. Does NOT block commits.

(go-linter-driven-development) BACKWARD view over rules/ — routes linter and review failures to the rule whose Fix pattern owns the repair.
Use when linter fails with complexity issues (cyclomatic, cognitive, maintainability) or when code feels hard to read/maintain.
Also runs PREPARATORY mode: reshape code an approved plan touches, before the first RED, so the feature lands add-only.
Applies storifying, type extraction, function extraction, conditional-dispatch, and mutation-discipline patterns via rules/R1-R8 and R10-R12.

Run standalone preparatory refactoring (Fowler: "make the change easy, then make the
easy change") for a change you're about to implement — without entering the full
five-phase workflow.

⏱️ **Estimated Duration**: 2–10 minutes (zero findings is the common case and takes seconds)

**Input**: a description of the impending change ("add an SMS channel to alerts",
"extend the exporter with histogram support"), optionally scoped to files. No
description → ask for one; preparation without a change in hand is just cleanup and
belongs to `/go-ldd-quickfix`.

**Steps** (the gate definitions live in @linter-driven-development
`<phase_1_5_prepare>` — apply them from there, never from memory):

1. **Locate touch points**: from the change description, identify the files,
   functions, and packages the change will extend or integrate with (grep for the
   named concepts; when ambiguous, invoke @code-designing briefly to sketch the
   landing zone).
2. **Survey**: run the rule detection greps (`../rules/R*.md` Falsifying questions)
   scoped to the touch points.
3. **Gate autonomously**: MULTIPLY → SAFE → BOUNDED → SKEPTICIZED, per
   @linter-driven-development `<phase_1_5_prepare>`. No user questions — the gates
   decide; deferred findings are reported, not asked about.

4	
5	A conditional that asks what a value *is* — a type switch, or a switch/if-chain on a
6	kind/status/mode discriminator — may exist **once**. The second copy of that
7	discriminator is a missing polymorphic type: the variants want to be implementations
8	of an interface (or entries in a dispatch map), chosen once at the boundary, so
9	downstream code *tells* the value what to do instead of asking what it is. One
10	well-placed, exhaustive switch is not a defect; a duplicated one always is.
11	
12	## Why
13	
14	Every `if (new kind) { new code }` doubles the execution paths through the function —
15	five conditionals means 32 paths to reason about and test. Worse, kind-switches
16	replicate: the same `switch msg.Channel` appears in send, validate, format, and retry
17	code, and adding a variant means finding and editing every copy — the one you miss is
18	the bug that ships. The compiler cannot help: an if-chain has no notion of
19	completeness, so a forgotten variant falls through silently. Dispatching once —
20	constructing the right implementation at the boundary (`R2-self-validating-types.md`
21	owns "validate once at the edge"; this rule is its behavioral twin: *decide* once at
22	the edge) — collapses N switches into one construction site, makes each variant a
23	leaf that unit-tests in isolation, and turns "add a variant" into "add a type" with
24	zero edits to existing code. This idea comes from the Anti-IF movement (Cirillo,
25	2007): the enemy is not `if`, it is the duplicated kind-conditional.

152	- **A kept switch must be exhaustive.** When one switch over a closed enum stays
153	  (single site, trivial variance), name the enum (`R1-primitive-obsession.md`,
154	  "Name enum strings"), drop the `default`, and let the `exhaustive` linter prove
155	  completeness — the linter then does what the if-chain never could: fail the build
156	  when a variant is added but not handled.
157	- **The over-abstraction trap, dispatch edition.** An interface with one production
158	  implementation is R6's territory; two trivial implementations behind one switch at
159	  one site score LOW on R1's juiciness scorecard — keep the conditional. Conditionals
160	  on *state/values* (`if n > threshold`, `if err != nil`, guard clauses per
161	  `R3-storifying.md`) are healthy control flow, not dispatch — this rule never
162	  touches them.
163	
164	## Fix pattern
165	
166	- **Replace Duplicated Switch with Interface Dispatch**: define the interface from the
167	  union of what all copies of the switch do (one method per switching site is a
168	  starting point, then collapse); one type per variant; move each `case` body into
169	  its variant; introduce `ParseX(raw) (X, error)` as the single decision point and
170	  migrate call sites to method calls. When the dispatch produces an output that
171	  carries fields the variants don't own (shared name/TLS on a wire request), give
172	  the interface a fill-style method (`fillUpdate(req *T)`) instead of a constructor —
173	  the caller owns the shared fields, each variant fills its own

175	- **Replace If-Chain with Strategy Map**: single-behavior variance → package-level
176	  `map[Kind]func(...)` (or a field), comma-ok on lookup at the boundary only.
177	- **Introduce Null Object**: absent-collaborator nil-checks → a no-op implementation
178	  constructed by default; delete the guards.
179	- **Split Flag Argument**: boolean/enum parameter that selects behavior → two named
180	  functions, or a variant type chosen by the caller's constructor.
181	- **Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch**: one site, closed enum → named enum type (R1),

183	  sanctioned form — record it as the decision, not a TODO.

188	  move is unavailable across the package boundary):

202

214	   to shrinking the switch to pure dispatch. `errors.As`/`errors.Is` chains and
215	   decode/unmarshal of foreign types are not this pattern.
216

219	   `errors.New`/`fmt.Errorf`/panic on an unknown-kind message.
220	   Violation: unknown-kind errors deep in the call graph — the maybe-unknown concept
221	   leaked past construction; dispatch should have been chosen at `ParseX`.
222

224	   Detection: `grep -nE 'func .*\(.*\b(is|use|with|enable|skip)[A-Za-z]* bool' $(git diff --name-only -- '*.go')`;

226	   Violation: a flag argument whose branches share little code — Split Flag Argument.

230	   implementations/entries and the number of sites the old conditional occupied

  constructed by default; delete the guards.
- **Split Flag Argument**: boolean/enum parameter that selects behavior → two named
  functions, or a variant type chosen by the caller's constructor.
- **Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch**: one site, closed enum → named enum type (R1),
  no `default`, `exhaustive` linter enforcing completeness. This is the rule's
  sanctioned form — record it as the decision, not a TODO.
- New types this creates must pass R1's juiciness scorecard, land per
  `R4-helper-placement.md`, and never become test-only interfaces
  (`R6-test-only-interfaces.md`). Rejection case law — juiciness (the switch stays,
  goes exhaustive): `../examples/anti-if-dispatch.md`; dependency direction (the
  move is unavailable across the package boundary):
  `../examples/switch-to-polymorphism.md`.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Is the same discriminator inspected in more than one place?**
   Detection: list discriminators in the diff —
   `grep -nE 'switch [a-zA-Z_.]+\.(Type|Kind|Status|Mode|Channel|Format|Level)\b' $(git diff --name-only -- '*.go')`
   and if-chain forms `grep -nE 'if [a-zA-Z_.]+\.(Type|Kind|Status|Mode|Channel|Format|Level) ==' ...`;
   then count each across the package: `grep -rn 'switch .*\.<Field>' --include='*.go' . | wc -l` (plus `== ` comparisons on the same field).
   Violation: ≥2 sites inspecting one discriminator — the decision has no single
   owner; route to Interface Dispatch or Strategy Map.

2. **Does a type switch dispatch on concrete types outside a boundary?**
   Detection: `grep -rn 'switch .* := .*\.(type)' --include='*.go' .` — for each hit,
   is it in a `ParseX`/decoder/boundary adapter, or in business logic?
   Violation: a type switch in domain logic whose cases call variant-specific
   behavior or unpack the variants' fields — the behavior belongs on the variants.
   A switch over an interface the *same package* owns is a violation even at a
   single site and even in a converter: the decision was already made at
   construction, and interface satisfaction gives the completeness proof a
   switch can't (`../examples/switch-to-polymorphism.md`). The boundary exemption
   applies only when the output format belongs to a *different* package than the
   cased types (that example's boundary counter) — there, the finding is limited
   to shrinking the switch to pure dispatch. `errors.As`/`errors.Is` chains and
   decode/unmarshal of foreign types are not this pattern.

3. **Does a `default:` (or trailing `else`) handle "unknown kind" away from the boundary?**
   Detection: for each switch found in Q1, check the `default` arm for
   `errors.New`/`fmt.Errorf`/panic on an unknown-kind message.
   Violation: unknown-kind errors deep in the call graph — the maybe-unknown concept
   leaked past construction; dispatch should have been chosen at `ParseX`.

4. **Does a boolean parameter select between behaviors?**
   Detection: `grep -nE 'func .*\(.*\b(is|use|with|enable|skip)[A-Za-z]* bool' $(git diff --name-only -- '*.go')`;
   check whether the function branches on it near the top.
   Violation: a flag argument whose branches share little code — Split Flag Argument.

5. **Inverse — is a NEW dispatch abstraction in the diff unearned?**
   Detection: for each new interface/strategy map in the diff, count production
   implementations/entries and the number of sites the old conditional occupied
   (`git log -p` or the pre-diff file).
   Violation: one switching site with trivial variance replaced by an interface —
   score it (R1 scorecard); if LOW, the finding is the *extraction*, and the fix is
   Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch. An interface whose second implementation exists
   only in tests is an R6 violation, not a dispatch win.

1	# R1 — Primitive Obsession
2	
3	## Principle
4	
5	Domain concepts must not travel as raw `string`/`int`/`bool`/`[]T`. When a primitive
6	carries validation rules, behavior, or a domain name, it becomes a type with a
7	validating constructor and named methods. The inverse binds equally: a wrapper that
8	adds no validation, no logic, and no invariant is over-abstraction — score before you wrap.
9	
10	## Why
11	
12	A rule enforced on a primitive is enforced at every call site and owned by none: the
13	check gets duplicated, drifts, and is skipped exactly once — in the code path that
14	ships the bug. Logic trapped on primitives is also untestable in isolation: you must
15	construct whatever large object happens to hold the primitive. A domain type gives the
16	rule one owner (the constructor — see `R2-self-validating-types.md`), gives the
17	behavior a name, makes invalid values unrepresentable downstream, and turns the logic
18	into a leaf that unit-tests with literals. Where the extracted type then lives is
19	`R4-helper-placement.md`.
20	
21	## Canonical example
22	
23	Real PR code (weka/goweka#951). `kubeService` wraps a Kubernetes Service DTO and must
24	pick the management port: prefer the port named `weka-api`, else fall back to the
25	first valid port.
26	
27	### Before
28	
29	```go
30	func (s kubeService) managementPort() int32 {
31	    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
32	        if p.Name == "weka-api" && p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
33	            return p.Port
34	        }
35	    }
36	    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
37	        if p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
38	            return p.Port
39	        }
40	    }
41	    return 0
42	}
43	```
44	
45	Four defects in twelve lines:
46	
47	- The validity rule `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` is duplicated across the two
48	  loops — two copies that can drift independently.
49	- Two abstractions exist only as unnamed boolean expressions: "valid port" and
50	  "named management port".
51	- The logic lives on a K8s DTO, so it is testable only by constructing a
52	  `kubeService` around a full Service object.
53	- `return 0` is a sentinel: validity is encoded in-band, and every caller must know
54	  that `0` means "none".
55	
56	### Stage 1 — self-validating types with constructors
57	
58	```go
59	// ServicePort is the wire DTO. Its fields stay exported with json tags —
60	// unexported fields with json tags silently fail to unmarshal (encoding/json
61	// skips them without error, and every port reads as zero).
62	type ServicePort struct {
63	    Name string `json:"name"`
64	    Port int32  `json:"port"`
65	}
66	
67	// Port is a named, validated service port. It cannot exist out of range,
68	// so no downstream code ever re-checks it.
69	type Port struct {
70	    name   string
71	    number int32
72	}
73	
74	func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
75	    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
76	        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
77	    }
78	    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
79	}
80	
81	func (p Port) Name() string  { return p.name }
82	func (p Port) Number() int32 { return p.number }
83	
84	// Ports is a collection of valid ports.
85	type Ports []Port
86	
87	// ParsePorts drops invalid wire entries — a documented decision that mirrors
88	// the original skip-and-fall-back semantics: an invalid port was never chosen
89	// before; now it never exists.
90	func ParsePorts(wire []ServicePort) Ports {
91	    ports := make(Ports, 0, len(wire))
92	    for _, w := range wire {
93	        p, err := ParsePort(w.Name, w.Port)
94	        if err != nil {
95	            continue
96	        }
97	        ports = append(ports, p)
98	    }
99	    return ports
100	}
101	
102	func (ps Ports) FirstNamed(name string) (Port, bool) {
103	    for _, p := range ps {
104	        if p.name == name {
105	            return p, true
106	        }
107	    }
108	    return Port{}, false
109	}
110	
111	func (ps Ports) First() (Port, bool) {
112	    if len(ps) == 0 {
113	        return Port{}, false
114	    }
115	    return ps[0], true
116	}
117	
118	// Management prefers the port named "weka-api", else the first valid port.
119	// (Stage 2 relocates this method — the "weka-api" preference is feature
120	// policy, not networking vocabulary.)
121	func (ps Ports) Management() (Port, bool) {
122	    if p, ok := ps.FirstNamed("weka-api"); ok {
123	        return p, true
124	    }
125	    return ps.First()
126	}
127	```
128	
129	The payoff, stated plainly: notice what was **not** written. There is no `IsValid()`
130	method and no validity loop anywhere. Self-validation does not move the
131	`> 0 && <= 65535` check somewhere tidier — it **deletes the concept of a
132	maybe-invalid port from downstream logic**. Every `Port` inside a `Ports` is valid by
133	construction, so "find the first valid port" collapses to "find the first port". And
134	`Management()` returns `(Port, bool)` comma-ok — never a `0` sentinel that smuggles
135	validity back in-band.
136	
137	### Stage 2 — placement (R4 rung 3)
138	
139	`Port`, `Ports`, `FirstNamed`, `First` say nothing about Kubernetes or Weka — they
140	are generic networking vocabulary, so they move to `internal/pkg/networking`
141	(rung 3 of `R4-helper-placement.md`). The wire adapter `ParsePorts` knows the K8s
142	DTO, so it stays with the feature. The feature policy stays home as a four-line
143	storified method:
144	
145	```go
146	func (s kubeService) managementPort() (networking.Port, bool) {
147	    if p, ok := s.ports.FirstNamed(kubeWekaAPIPort); ok { return p, true }
148	    return s.ports.First()
149	}
150	```
151	
152	Teaching point: **promote only the domain-generic parts.** The `"weka-api"` constant
153	is feature policy and stays in the feature — a shared package that knows one
154	feature's port names is not shared vocabulary, it is leaked policy.
155	
156	### Stage 3 — testing contrast
157	
158	Before, exercising `managementPort()` meant constructing a `kubeService` around a
159	full Service fixture — building a Kubernetes object to check a range predicate.
160	After, the logic is a leaf and its rung-0 unit tests (the composition ladder's
161	bottom rung — see @testing) are slice literals against `networking.Ports`; no
162	big-object construction:
163	
164	```go
165	func TestPorts_FirstNamed(t *testing.T) {
166	    api := mustPort(t, "weka-api", 14000)
167	    web := mustPort(t, "http", 80)
168	
169	    got, ok := networking.Ports{web, api}.FirstNamed("weka-api")
170	
171	    require.True(t, ok)
172	    assert.Equal(t, api, got)
173	}
174	
175	func mustPort(t *testing.T, name string, number int32) networking.Port {
176	    t.Helper()
177	    p, err := networking.ParsePort(name, number)
178	    require.NoError(t, err)
179	    return p
180	}
181	```
182	
183	### The opposite failure: don't over-extract
184	
185	```go
186	// ❌ Ceremony, not a type: no rule, no behavior — the only method unwraps.
187	type ReplicaCount int
188	
189	func (c ReplicaCount) Int() int { return int(c) }
190	```
191	
192	Score it against the scorecard below: no validation (+0), no meaningful methods (+0),
193	one call site (+0) → Score 0. Keep the `int`; if you want a name, a well-named
194	variable or an unexported helper in the same package is the whole answer
195	(`R4-helper-placement.md`, rung 1). Deep worked rejection with the cheaper
196	alternatives: `../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.
197	
198	## Design guidance
199	
200	A primitive should become a type when it has validation rules, has behavior attached,
201	represents a domain concept, is used in multiple places, or when passing an invalid
202	value would be a bug. When the call is not obvious, score it.
203	
204	### Juiciness scoring
205	
206	This scorecard lives here and only here — other rules and skills cite it, never
207	restate it.
208	
209	**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
210	- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
211	- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
212	- State transitions/transformations: +2
213	- Format conversions: +1
214	
215	**Structural (organizing complexity):**
216	- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
217	- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
218	- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
219	- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2
220	
221	**Usage (simplifies code):**
222	- Used in 5+ places: +2
223	- Used in 3-4 places: +1
224	- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
225	- Makes tests cleaner: +1
226	
227	**Verdict:**
228	- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
229	- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
230	- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.
231	
232	### The over-abstraction trap
233	
234	The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
235	nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
236	honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
237	accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
238	private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type. Deep worked case — the tried
239	extraction, the rejection rationale, and the cheaper alternatives:
240	`../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.
241	
242	### Placement
243	
244	A juicy type must also land in the right package — feature-scoped versus
245	domain-generic. That decision is `R4-helper-placement.md`; the canonical example's
246	Stage 2 shows it applied.
247	
248	## Fix pattern
249	
250	- **Replace Primitive with Domain Type**: introduce `ParseX(raw) (X, error)`
251	  (`R2-self-validating-types.md`); migrate call sites so raw values cross into `X`
252	  exactly once, at the boundary.
253	- **Extract Collection Type**: when logic loops over `[]primitive` or `[]DTO`, wrap
254	  the slice (`type Ports []Port`) and move the loop into a named query method.
255	- **Replace Sentinel with comma-ok**: `return 0` / `return ""` meaning
256	  absence/invalidity → `(X, bool)` or `(X, error)`.
257	- **Name enum strings**: `if status == "READY"` → `type Status string` with
258	  `const StatusReady Status = "READY"`.
259	- **Introduce Parameter Object** (Fowler): the same group of parameters traveling
260	  through multiple signatures (`host string, port int, useTLS bool`) becomes one
261	  type — that is the scorecard's "grouping related data that travels together" made
262	  concrete. Prefer passing the whole object over re-exploding its fields at the next
263	  call (Preserve Whole Object).
264	- **Over-abstraction found instead?** Apply the cheaper alternative — better naming,

# R1 — Primitive Obsession

## Principle

Domain concepts must not travel as raw `string`/`int`/`bool`/`[]T`. When a primitive
carries validation rules, behavior, or a domain name, it becomes a type with a
validating constructor and named methods. The inverse binds equally: a wrapper that
adds no validation, no logic, and no invariant is over-abstraction — score before you wrap.

## Why

A rule enforced on a primitive is enforced at every call site and owned by none: the
check gets duplicated, drifts, and is skipped exactly once — in the code path that
ships the bug. Logic trapped on primitives is also untestable in isolation: you must
construct whatever large object happens to hold the primitive. A domain type gives the
rule one owner (the constructor — see `R2-self-validating-types.md`), gives the
behavior a name, makes invalid values unrepresentable downstream, and turns the logic
into a leaf that unit-tests with literals. Where the extracted type then lives is
`R4-helper-placement.md`.

## Canonical example

Real PR code (weka/goweka#951). `kubeService` wraps a Kubernetes Service DTO and must
pick the management port: prefer the port named `weka-api`, else fall back to the
first valid port.

### Before

```go
func (s kubeService) managementPort() int32 {
    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
        if p.Name == "weka-api" && p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
            return p.Port
        }
    }
    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
        if p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
            return p.Port
        }
    }
    return 0
}
```

Four defects in twelve lines:

- The validity rule `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` is duplicated across the two
  loops — two copies that can drift independently.
- Two abstractions exist only as unnamed boolean expressions: "valid port" and
  "named management port".
- The logic lives on a K8s DTO, so it is testable only by constructing a
  `kubeService` around a full Service object.
- `return 0` is a sentinel: validity is encoded in-band, and every caller must know
  that `0` means "none".

### Stage 1 — self-validating types with constructors

```go
// ServicePort is the wire DTO. Its fields stay exported with json tags —
// unexported fields with json tags silently fail to unmarshal (encoding/json
// skips them without error, and every port reads as zero).
type ServicePort struct {
    Name string `json:"name"`
    Port int32  `json:"port"`
}

// Port is a named, validated service port. It cannot exist out of range,
// so no downstream code ever re-checks it.
type Port struct {
    name   string
    number int32
}

func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
    }
    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
}

func (p Port) Name() string  { return p.name }
func (p Port) Number() int32 { return p.number }

// Ports is a collection of valid ports.
type Ports []Port

// ParsePorts drops invalid wire entries — a documented decision that mirrors
// the original skip-and-fall-back semantics: an invalid port was never chosen
// before; now it never exists.
func ParsePorts(wire []ServicePort) Ports {
    ports := make(Ports, 0, len(wire))
    for _, w := range wire {
        p, err := ParsePort(w.Name, w.Port)
        if err != nil {
            continue
        }
        ports = append(ports, p)
    }
    return ports
}

func (ps Ports) FirstNamed(name string) (Port, bool) {
    for _, p := range ps {
        if p.name == name {
            return p, true
        }
    }
    return Port{}, false
}

func (ps Ports) First() (Port, bool) {
    if len(ps) == 0 {
        return Port{}, false
    }
    return ps[0], true
}

// Management prefers the port named "weka-api", else the first valid port.
// (Stage 2 relocates this method — the "weka-api" preference is feature
// policy, not networking vocabulary.)
func (ps Ports) Management() (Port, bool) {
    if p, ok := ps.FirstNamed("weka-api"); ok {
        return p, true
    }
    return ps.First()
}
```

The payoff, stated plainly: notice what was **not** written. There is no `IsValid()`
method and no validity loop anywhere. Self-validation does not move the
`> 0 && <= 65535` check somewhere tidier — it **deletes the concept of a
maybe-invalid port from downstream logic**. Every `Port` inside a `Ports` is valid by
construction, so "find the first valid port" collapses to "find the first port". And
`Management()` returns `(Port, bool)` comma-ok — never a `0` sentinel that smuggles
validity back in-band.

### Stage 2 — placement (R4 rung 3)

`Port`, `Ports`, `FirstNamed`, `First` say nothing about Kubernetes or Weka — they
are generic networking vocabulary, so they move to `internal/pkg/networking`
(rung 3 of `R4-helper-placement.md`). The wire adapter `ParsePorts` knows the K8s
DTO, so it stays with the feature. The feature policy stays home as a four-line
storified method:

```go
func (s kubeService) managementPort() (networking.Port, bool) {
    if p, ok := s.ports.FirstNamed(kubeWekaAPIPort); ok { return p, true }
    return s.ports.First()
}
```

Teaching point: **promote only the domain-generic parts.** The `"weka-api"` constant
is feature policy and stays in the feature — a shared package that knows one
feature's port names is not shared vocabulary, it is leaked policy.

### Stage 3 — testing contrast

Before, exercising `managementPort()` meant constructing a `kubeService` around a
full Service fixture — building a Kubernetes object to check a range predicate.
After, the logic is a leaf and its rung-0 unit tests (the composition ladder's
bottom rung — see @testing) are slice literals against `networking.Ports`; no
big-object construction:

```go
func TestPorts_FirstNamed(t *testing.T) {
    api := mustPort(t, "weka-api", 14000)
    web := mustPort(t, "http", 80)

    got, ok := networking.Ports{web, api}.FirstNamed("weka-api")

    require.True(t, ok)
    assert.Equal(t, api, got)
}

func mustPort(t *testing.T, name string, number int32) networking.Port {
    t.Helper()
    p, err := networking.ParsePort(name, number)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    return p
}
```

### The opposite failure: don't over-extract

```go
// ❌ Ceremony, not a type: no rule, no behavior — the only method unwraps.
type ReplicaCount int

func (c ReplicaCount) Int() int { return int(c) }
```

Score it against the scorecard below: no validation (+0), no meaningful methods (+0),
one call site (+0) → Score 0. Keep the `int`; if you want a name, a well-named
variable or an unexported helper in the same package is the whole answer
(`R4-helper-placement.md`, rung 1). Deep worked rejection with the cheaper
alternatives: `../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.

## Design guidance

A primitive should become a type when it has validation rules, has behavior attached,
represents a domain concept, is used in multiple places, or when passing an invalid
value would be a bug. When the call is not obvious, score it.

### Juiciness scoring

This scorecard lives here and only here — other rules and skills cite it, never
restate it.

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

### The over-abstraction trap

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type. Deep worked case — the tried
extraction, the rejection rationale, and the cheaper alternatives:
`../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.

### Placement

A juicy type must also land in the right package — feature-scoped versus
domain-generic. That decision is `R4-helper-placement.md`; the canonical example's
Stage 2 shows it applied.

## Fix pattern

- **Replace Primitive with Domain Type**: introduce `ParseX(raw) (X, error)`
  (`R2-self-validating-types.md`); migrate call sites so raw values cross into `X`
  exactly once, at the boundary.
- **Extract Collection Type**: when logic loops over `[]primitive` or `[]DTO`, wrap
  the slice (`type Ports []Port`) and move the loop into a named query method.
- **Replace Sentinel with comma-ok**: `return 0` / `return ""` meaning
  absence/invalidity → `(X, bool)` or `(X, error)`.
- **Name enum strings**: `if status == "READY"` → `type Status string` with
  `const StatusReady Status = "READY"`.
- **Introduce Parameter Object** (Fowler): the same group of parameters traveling
  through multiple signatures (`host string, port int, useTLS bool`) becomes one
  type — that is the scorecard's "grouping related data that travels together" made
  concrete. Prefer passing the whole object over re-exploding its fields at the next
  call (Preserve Whole Object).
- **Over-abstraction found instead?** Apply the cheaper alternative — better naming,
  or private fields + accessors — per `../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.
- Multi-rule refactoring procedure (sequencing extraction with storifying):
  `../skills/refactoring/reference.md`. Forward design of the new types:
  @code-designing.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Does the diff validate a primitive inline instead of constructing a type?**
   Detection: `grep -nE 'if [a-zA-Z_.]+ (==|!=) ""|if [a-zA-Z_.]+ (<=?|>=?) [0-9]' $(git diff --name-only -- '*.go')`
   Violation: an emptiness/range/format check on a parameter or DTO field that names
   a domain concept (port, id, email, path, addr), outside a `ParseX`/`NewX`
   constructor.

2. **Is the same predicate enforced in more than one place?**
   Detection: for each predicate found above, grep its normalized form across the
   package, e.g. `grep -rn '> 0 && .*<= 65535' --include='*.go' .` — count hits.
   Violation: ≥2 hits — the rule has no single owner; a type is missing.

3. **Does named behavior run on a bare primitive?** Loops/switches over `[]string`,
   string-literal status comparisons, format logic on a `string` field.
   Detection: `grep -rnE '== "[A-Z_]+"' --include='*.go' .` for enum-shaped
   comparisons; inspect diff for loops whose body interprets a primitive.
   Violation: behavior attached to a bare primitive where a named method on a type
   would carry it.

4. **Does any function return a sentinel to mean "not found / invalid"?**
   Detection: grep the diff for `return 0`, `return ""`, `return -1` in functions
   whose signature has no `bool` or `error` result.
   Violation: validity encoded in-band — requires comma-ok or `(X, error)`.

5. **Do the same parameters travel together across signatures?**
   Detection: for each changed function with ≥3 parameters, grep the package for the
   same parameter-name pair/trio in other signatures, e.g.
   `grep -rnE 'func .*host string.*port int' --include='*.go' .`
   Violation: the same group of ≥2–3 parameters co-occurs in ≥2 signatures — a data
   clump; Introduce Parameter Object (score it: grouping-that-travels is +2 on the
   scorecard, plus its usage points).

6. **Inverse — is a NEW type in the diff mere ceremony?**
   Detection: count its methods (`grep -c 'func ([a-z0-9]* *\*\?<Type>)' <file>`) and
   check whether any method does more than unwrap or rename the primitive; score it
   with the scorecard above.
   Violation: Score 0-1, or the only method is `return <primitive>(x)` —
   over-abstraction; the finding must cite the cheaper alternative
   (`../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`).

1	# Anti-IF Dispatch Case: One Decision, One Owner
2	
3	Demonstrates: R11 (edges into R1, R2, R6)
4	
5	A worked study of the R11 moves on a realistic alert-notification slice: a string
6	discriminator inspected in three files becomes an interface chosen once at the
7	boundary; a single-function variance becomes a strategy map instead; and the inverse
8	case — where the skeptic kills the extraction and the switch *stays* — is worked to
9	its cheaper alternative. The compact excerpt lives in
10	`../rules/R11-conditional-dispatch.md`; this file is the full case law.
11	
12	## The disease: a decision with three owners
13	
14	The alert feature delivers over email, Slack, or PagerDuty. `Alert.Channel` is a raw
15	string (already an R1 smell), and three sites ask what it is:
16	
17	```go
18	// ❌ alert/send.go
19	func Send(a Alert) error {
20	    switch a.Channel {
21	    case "email":
22	        return smtpSend(a.Recipient, renderEmail(a))
23	    case "slack":
24	        return slackPost(a.Recipient, renderSlack(a))
25	    case "pagerduty":
26	        return pdCreateIncident(a.Recipient, a.Summary)
27	    default:
28	        return fmt.Errorf("unknown channel %q", a.Channel)
29	    }
30	}
31	
32	// ❌ alert/validate.go — drifted: pagerduty was never added here
33	func validRecipient(a Alert) bool {
34	    switch a.Channel {
35	    case "email":
36	        return strings.Contains(a.Recipient, "@")
37	    case "slack":
38	        return strings.HasPrefix(a.Recipient, "#")
39	    }
40	    return false
41	}
42	
43	// ❌ alert/retry.go — the same decision wearing an if-chain
44	func retryDelay(a Alert) time.Duration {
45	    if a.Channel == "pagerduty" {
46	        return 0
47	    }
48	    if a.Channel == "slack" {
49	        return 5 * time.Second
50	    }
51	    return time.Minute
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Why this is a defect and not a style choice:
56	
57	- **The drift already happened.** `validRecipient` returns `false` for `"pagerduty"`
58	  — not by decision, but because the second copy of the switch was not in view when
59	  the third channel landed. Duplicated discriminators drift the same way duplicated
60	  validation predicates drift (R1's Q2).
61	- **Adding SMS is a scavenger hunt.** Three known sites, plus whatever a grep misses
62	  (test helpers, a metrics label formatter). The compiler flags none of them: an
63	  if-chain has no completeness, and a switch with a `default` swallows the new case
64	  silently.
65	- **"Unknown channel" leaks everywhere.** Every switching site carries the
66	  `default:`/fall-through arm, so every function's signature and tests carry the
67	  maybe-unknown concept — the behavioral twin of R1's maybe-invalid port.
68	- **Nothing unit-tests in isolation.** Slack's recipient rule is only reachable by
69	  driving `validRecipient` with a fully built `Alert`.
70	
71	## Move 1 — Replace Duplicated Switch with Interface Dispatch
72	
73	Define the interface from the union of what the copies do: `Send` switches on
74	delivery, `validRecipient` on addressing, `retryDelay` on retry policy — three
75	methods, one type per variant:
76	
77	```go
78	// alert/channel.go
79	type Channel interface {
80	    Send(a Alert) error
81	    ValidRecipient(recipient string) bool
82	    RetryDelay() time.Duration
83	}
84	
85	// ParseChannel is the single decision point. This switch is ALLOWED —
86	// it is the one place the raw string may be inspected (R11), exactly as
87	// a ParseX constructor is the one place a raw value is validated (R2).
88	func ParseChannel(name string) (Channel, error) {
89	    switch name {
90	    case "email":
91	        return Email{}, nil
92	    case "slack":
93	        return Slack{}, nil
94	    case "pagerduty":
95	        return PagerDuty{}, nil
96	    default:
97	        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown channel %q", name)
98	    }
99	}
100	```
101	
102	```go
103	// alert/slack.go — each variant is a leaf type owning ALL its behavior
104	type Slack struct{}
105	
106	func (Slack) Send(a Alert) error           { return slackPost(a.Recipient, renderSlack(a)) }
107	func (Slack) ValidRecipient(r string) bool { return strings.HasPrefix(r, "#") }
108	func (Slack) RetryDelay() time.Duration    { return 5 * time.Second }
109	```
110	
111	`Alert` now holds a `Channel`, constructed at the boundary (the HTTP handler or
112	config loader calls `ParseChannel` and fails fast there). The three switching sites
113	collapse to method calls:
114	
115	```go
116	func Send(a Alert) error            { return a.Channel.Send(a) }
117	func validRecipient(a Alert) bool   { return a.Channel.ValidRecipient(a.Recipient) }
118	func retryDelay(a Alert) time.Duration { return a.Channel.RetryDelay() }
119	```
120	
121	(And once they are one-liners, the wrappers themselves usually dissolve into their
122	callers — the story functions call the methods directly, R3.)
123	
124	What was deleted, not relocated: every `default:` arm downstream. An `Alert` that
125	exists holds a `Channel` that exists; "unknown channel" is unrepresentable past
126	`ParseChannel`. Adding SMS is now one new file (`sms.go`) plus one `case` in
127	`ParseChannel` — no existing file changes.
128	
129	**R6 check, answered explicitly:** this interface is *earned* — it has three
130	production implementations on day one. R6 forbids interfaces whose only second
131	implementer is a test double; a dispatch interface born with one variant "for the
132	future" fails that test and should stay a switch until the second variant is real.
133	
134	### The testing payoff
135	
136	Each variant unit-tests as a leaf with literals — no `Alert` construction, no
137	switch-driving:
138	
139	```go
140	func TestSlack_ValidRecipient(t *testing.T) {
141	    assert.True(t, alert.Slack{}.ValidRecipient("#oncall"))
142	    assert.False(t, alert.Slack{}.ValidRecipient("oncall"))
143	}
144	
145	func TestParseChannel_Unknown(t *testing.T) {
146	    _, err := alert.ParseChannel("carrier-pigeon")
147	    require.Error(t, err)
148	}
149	```
150	
151	The drift bug (`pagerduty` missing from `validRecipient`) can no longer be written:
152	there is no second place to forget.
153	
154	## Move 2 — Replace If-Chain with Strategy Map
155	
156	Not every variance deserves an interface. Suppose only *rendering* varies by an
157	output format, in one behavioral dimension:
158	
159	```go
160	// ❌ before: if-chain in the middle of business logic
161	func render(a Alert, format string) string {
162	    if format == "json" {
163	        return renderJSON(a)
164	    }
165	    if format == "text" {
166	        return renderText(a)
167	    }
168	    return renderMarkdown(a) // silent default — is "yaml" markdown? nobody decided
169	}
170	```
171	
172	One behavior → a map, not three types:
173	
174	```go
175	type Format string
176	
177	const (
178	    FormatJSON     Format = "json"
179	    FormatText     Format = "text"
180	    FormatMarkdown Format = "markdown"
181	)
182	
183	var renderers = map[Format]func(Alert) string{
184	    FormatJSON:     renderJSON,
185	    FormatText:     renderText,
186	    FormatMarkdown: renderMarkdown,
187	}
188	
189	func ParseFormat(raw string) (Format, error) {
190	    if _, ok := renderers[Format(raw)]; !ok {
191	        return "", fmt.Errorf("unknown format %q", raw)
192	    }
193	    return Format(raw), nil
194	}
195	
196	func render(a Alert, f Format) string { return renderers[f](a) }
197	```
198	
199	The lookup *is* the dispatch; the comma-ok check lives once, in `ParseFormat`, at the
200	boundary. The silent markdown default — an undecided decision — became an explicit
201	error. (The map is package-level immutable data, the sanctioned shape under R8;
202	naming the enum is R1's "Name enum strings" move.)
203	
204	## Move 3 — the rejection: when the switch stays
205	
206	The skeptic's side of R11, worked honestly. The same codebase has this:
207	
208	```go
209	// alert/severity.go — the ONLY site that inspects Severity
210	func (s Severity) Color() string {
211	    switch s {
212	    case SeverityInfo:
213	        return "blue"
214	    case SeverityWarning:
215	        return "yellow"
216	    case SeverityCritical:
217	        return "red"
218	    }
219	    return ""
220	}
221	```
222	
223	A dispatch-happy reading says: three variants, extract `type Severity interface`
224	with `Info`, `Warning`, `Critical` types. Score it before moving (R1 scorecard, via
225	the over-abstraction skeptic):
226	
227	- Duplication of the discriminator: **1 site** (grep `switch .*Severity` → one hit) — +0
228	- Behavioral variance: one method, returns a constant string — trivial — +0
229	- Would the interface be earned (R6)? Three implementations, but each is an empty
230	  struct wrapping one literal — ceremony
231	
232	Verdict: **REFUTED.** The extraction would turn 12 readable lines into three files
233	and an interface for zero deletion — no duplicated switch exists to delete. The
234	cheaper alternative is R11's sanctioned form, **Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch**:
235	
236	```go
237	func (s Severity) Color() string {
238	    switch s { // exhaustive: linter fails the build when a Severity is added unhandled
239	    case SeverityInfo:
240	        return "blue"
241	    case SeverityWarning:
242	        return "yellow"
243	    case SeverityCritical:
244	        return "red"
245	    }
246	    return ""
247	}
248	```
249	
250	with `exhaustive` enabled in `.golangci.yaml`. Now the linter provides what dispatch
251	would have: adding `SeverityFatal` fails the build at this switch instead of falling
252	through to `""`. That is the whole benefit, at none of the cost.
253	
254	**The dividing line, restated:** dispatch is bought with the *deletion of duplicated
255	decisions*. Three sites collapsed to one boundary — clear win (Move 1). One
256	single-dimension variance — a map (Move 2). One site, trivial variance — the switch
257	stays, made exhaustive (Move 3). If nothing gets deleted, the abstraction is
258	ceremony.
